title: Does temperature move sales?
equation: Predicted daily net sales = b0 + b1[Maximum temperature]

questions.text: Predict daily net sales for a day with maximum temperature of 66 degrees Fahrenheit.
questions.say: State the equation, substitute each value, and give the unit. Mention that the prediction is only as good as the model's fit.

questions.text: Interpret the coefficient on Maximum temperature.
questions.answer: Each additional degree Fahrenheit of maximum temperature is associated with an increase of 7.81 dollars in daily net sales.
questions.say: Give direction, size and unit, and say 'associated with' rather than 'causes'.

questions.text: Is the effect of Maximum temperature statistically significant at the 5% level? Explain to Bob what that means.
questions.answer: With a p-value of 0.006, maximum temperature is statistically significant at the 5% level: the p-value is below 0.05, so an effect this large would be unlikely if the true effect were zero.
questions.say: Compare the p-value with 0.05, then translate it into plain language for a restaurant owner. Not significant does not prove there is no effect.

questions.text: The model's R-squared is 0.024 with 309 daily observations. How confident should Bob be in predictions from this model?
questions.answer: The model explains 2.4% of the day-to-day variation in daily net sales, leaving 97.6% unexplained. Predictions will often miss by a wide margin, so Bob should treat them as a rough guide.
questions.say: Translate R-squared into 'share of variation explained', then give a practical judgement about ordering ingredients and scheduling staff.

questions.text: How does a game day change the relationship between sales 364 days ago and daily net sales?
questions.answer: On a day without a game, each additional dollar of sales 364 days ago is associated with a change of 0.619 dollars. On a game day the slope becomes 0.619 + (0.0113) = 0.6303, and the starting level shifts by 385 dollars. The interaction's p-value is 0.943, so the difference in slopes is not statistically significant at the 5% level.
questions.say: Explain that the interaction coefficient changes the slope, while the dummy coefficient changes the starting level. Check the interaction's p-value before leaning on it.
